title: Producers, Consumers and Choices
bigQuestion: Why can't we have everything we want, and how do people decide what to make, buy and share?

story.title: The Day the Pencils Ran Out
story.kicker: A fifth-grade store sells out in one morning, and the class discovers what a price is for.
paragraphs: Room 210 runs a small store. Every Friday morning the fifth graders sell pencils, erasers and notebooks from a table by the door. Maya keeps the money box. Devon counts the stock. A pencil costs ten cents. Most Fridays the store is quiet and the class makes a few dollars for a field trip.

One Friday in October, a big test is coming. Everyone wants a new pencil. By nine-thirty the line runs down the hall. By ten o'clock the tray is empty. Devon holds it up. "We are out," he says. Kids groan. Some walk away with nothing, and a few of them have a test in an hour.

At the class meeting, Ms. Alvarez asks one question. "Why did we run out?" Maya says they only ordered two hundred pencils. Devon says they should have ordered more. Priya says something different. "We sold them too cheap. Everybody bought three. Nobody needs three pencils."

The class argues about it. If a pencil cost twenty-five cents, fewer kids would grab three. The pencils would last all morning. But some kids only have a dime. Is a higher price fair to them? Ms. Alvarez smiles. "You are doing economics right now," she says.

The next Friday the class tries something new. They order four hundred pencils and set the price at fifteen cents. The line is shorter. Every kid who wants a pencil gets one, and a few are left over. The class learns that a price is a kind of message. It tells buyers and sellers what to do next.
story.think: Was raising the price fair? What else could the class have done so that every kid got a pencil?

lessons.title: Producers and Consumers
lessons.mainIdea: Producers make goods or do services, and consumers buy and use them; most people are both.
reading: Think about a loaf of bread. A farmer grew the wheat. A mill ground it into flour. A baker mixed the dough and baked it. A truck driver carried it to the store. Each of those people is a *producer*. A producer is anyone who makes something or does work that others want.

Now think about who eats the bread. You do. The person who buys a loaf and uses it is a *consumer*. A consumer is someone who buys or uses goods and services. When you buy a pencil at the school store, you are a consumer. When your family buys gas for the car, they are consumers too.

Here is the surprising part. Almost everyone is both. The baker is a producer at work. On the way home, she buys shoes, so she is a consumer. Devon is a producer when he runs the store table. He is a consumer when he buys a pencil from it. Producers and consumers need each other.

words.d: a person or business that makes goods or does services that others want
a person who buys or uses goods and services

look.title: One Morning, Two Jobs
look.text: Mr. Kim fixes bikes in a shop on Western Avenue. At seven in the morning he buys coffee and a bagel. At eight he opens his shop and fixes a flat tire for a customer. At noon he buys lunch from the taco truck. At three he sells a used bike to a teenager.
look.prompt: List each moment when Mr. Kim is a producer and each moment when he is a consumer.

check.q: Which person is acting as a producer?
choices: A baker making bread to sell
check.why: A producer makes goods or does work that others want. The baker is making bread to sell.

check.q: When Devon buys a pencil at the store, what is he?
check.why: A consumer buys or uses goods and services. Buying a pencil makes Devon a consumer.

check.q: Why does the lesson say most people are both producers and consumers?
choices: Because only bakers can buy bread
Because people work and also buy things
check.why: People produce at their jobs and consume when they buy food, shoes and other things.

lessons.title: Goods and Services
lessons.mainIdea: Goods are things you can hold; services are work someone does for you.
reading: Walk through a shopping street. In one window there are shoes, bread and toys. Those are *goods*. A good is a thing you can touch and take home. A pencil is a good. So is a bike, an apple or a video game disc. Producers make goods in factories, on farms and in kitchens.

Next door is a barber shop. The barber does not sell you a thing to carry away. He cuts your hair. That is a *service*. A service is work that one person does for another. A doctor's visit, a bus ride, a haircut and a dog-walk are all services. Teachers, nurses and mail carriers all sell services.

Sometimes a business sells both. A pizza shop sells a pizza, which is a good. If the shop delivers it to your door, that delivery is a service. In Chicago, a huge share of jobs are in services, like health care, offices, restaurants and trucking. Fewer people make goods than in the past.

words.d: a thing that can be made, bought and touched, like a pencil or a bike
work that a person does for someone else, like a haircut or a bus ride

look.title: A Saturday List
look.text: On Saturday, Rosa's family bought a bag of apples, paid the dentist for a check-up, bought a new soccer ball, paid a plumber to fix a leaking sink and took the CTA bus downtown.
look.prompt: Sort each thing the family paid for into goods or services. Which list is longer?

check.q: Which of these is a service?
check.why: A service is work done for someone else. A haircut is work the barber does for you.

check.q: What is a good?
choices: A thing you can touch and take home
check.why: A good is a thing that can be made and touched, like an apple or a bike.

check.q: A pizza shop delivers a pizza to your house. What has it sold you?
check.why: The pizza is a good. The delivery is a service. The shop sold both.

lessons.title: Scarcity and the Choice You Give Up
lessons.mainIdea: Nothing is unlimited, so every choice means giving up the next best thing, called the opportunity cost.
reading: Maya has two dollars. She wants a notebook that costs two dollars and a pack of stickers that costs two dollars. She cannot buy both. This problem has a name: *scarcity*. Scarcity means there is not enough of something to do everything people want. Money is scarce. So is time, land and water.

Because of scarcity, every choice has a cost that is not printed on a tag. If Maya buys the notebook, she gives up the stickers. The stickers are her *opportunity cost*. The opportunity cost of a choice is the next best thing you did not pick. It is what you gave up.

Families, businesses and cities face this too. A city has a fixed budget. If it spends money on a new pool, it may not fix a street that year. The street is the opportunity cost of the pool. Good choosers name the opportunity cost out loud before they decide. That way they know what they are trading.

words.d: not having enough of something to do everything people want
the next best thing you give up when you make a choice

look.title: One Free Hour
look.text: Jalen has one free hour after dinner. He could practice piano, play basketball at the park, or finish a puzzle with his little sister. He picks basketball. The hour is gone.
look.prompt: What was the opportunity cost of Jalen's choice? Why can it only be one thing, not two?

check.q: What does scarcity mean?
choices: Not enough of something for all that people want
check.why: Scarcity means there is not enough of something, like money or time, to do everything people want.

check.q: Maya buys the notebook instead of the stickers. What is her opportunity cost?
check.why: The opportunity cost is the next best thing given up. Maya gave up the stickers.

check.q: A city spends its money on a pool and cannot fix a street. What is the street?
choices: The opportunity cost of the pool
check.why: The street repair is what the city gave up to build the pool. That is its opportunity cost.

lessons.title: Demand at the School Store
lessons.mainIdea: Demand is how much people want to buy at a price; when the price drops, more people buy.
reading: On the Friday of the big test, everyone wanted pencils. That wanting, joined with the money to pay, is called *demand*. Demand is how much of something people will buy at a certain price. On a normal Friday, demand for pencils is low. On test day, it shoots up.

Price changes demand too. At ten cents, kids bought three pencils each. At twenty-five cents, most would buy one. When the price goes down, people buy more. When the price goes up, people buy less. That pattern is so steady that economists call it a law.

Demand can also change for reasons that have nothing to do with price. A test makes demand rise. A snow day makes it fall to zero. If a famous singer holds a pencil in a video, demand might jump. A *market* is any place where buyers and sellers meet, and the school store is a tiny one.

words.d: how much of something people want and are able to buy at a price
any place where buyers and sellers come together to trade

look.title: Lemonade in Two Weathers
look.text: Two kids run a lemonade stand at fifty cents a cup. On a cool, cloudy day they sell six cups. On a hot day the next week, at the same price, they sell thirty cups. Then they raise the price to a dollar on another hot day and sell fifteen.
look.prompt: What changed demand between the first two days? What changed it on the third day?

check.q: What is demand?
choices: How much people will buy at a price
How many items a store has
The cost of making a good
check.why: Demand is how much of a good people want and can buy at a certain price.

check.q: If the price of a pencil goes up, what usually happens to the number sold?
check.why: When price rises, people buy less. That is the pattern the lesson calls a law.

check.q: Why did demand for pencils rise on test day?
choices: More kids wanted pencils that day
check.why: A test made more kids want pencils. Demand rose for a reason other than price.

lessons.title: Supply and Running Out
lessons.mainIdea: Supply is how much sellers offer; when supply is low and demand is high, the price tends to rise.
reading: The class had two hundred pencils. That number is the *supply*. Supply is how much of something sellers are ready to sell at a price. Sellers like higher prices. If pencils sold for a dollar, the class would order more boxes. If they sold for a penny, the class might not bother.

Now put supply and demand together. On test day, demand was high and supply was small. That is when a store runs out. The line got long. Some kids left empty-handed. A *shortage* is when buyers want more than sellers have at that price.

A higher price fixes a shortage in two ways. It makes some buyers take fewer. It makes sellers bring more. When the class raised the price to fifteen cents and ordered four hundred pencils, supply went up and demand went down. They met in the middle. That is what markets do every day, all over the world.

words.d: how much of something sellers are ready to sell at a price
when buyers want more of something than sellers have at that price

look.title: The Snow Shovel Problem
look.text: A hardware store in Rockford has twenty snow shovels. A storm drops a foot of snow overnight. By noon, two hundred people have come in asking for shovels. The owner has to decide what to do with the twenty on the shelf.
look.prompt: What is happening to demand and supply? What could the owner do, and who would be helped or hurt?

check.q: What is supply?
choices: How much sellers are ready to sell at a price
check.why: Supply is the amount sellers are willing to offer at a certain price.

check.q: What is a shortage?
choices: Too many pencils on the shelf
A day when the store is closed
A price that is too high
Buyers want more than sellers have at that price
check.why: A shortage happens when demand is greater than supply at the current price.

check.q: How does a higher price help end a shortage?
choices: Buyers take fewer and sellers bring more
check.why: A higher price makes some buyers take less and gives sellers a reason to supply more.

lessons.title: What a Price Tells You
lessons.mainIdea: A price is a signal that tells buyers how to spend and sellers what to make.
reading: A *price* is the amount of money you trade for a good or service. But a price is also a message. When strawberries cost six dollars a box in January, the price says they are hard to get right now. In June, when Illinois farms are picking, the price drops to two dollars. The price says: plenty here, buy now.

Sellers read prices too. When pencils sold out fast at ten cents, the price was telling the class it was set too low. When the price of corn is high, farmers plant more corn. When it falls, some switch to soybeans. No one has to order them. The price does the talking.

Prices are not perfect. A price does not say whether something is good for you. It does not say whether a family can afford it. That is why people also use rules, taxes and help for people in need. But as a quick way to move goods to the people who want them most, a price is a powerful tool.

words.d: the amount of money traded for a good or service
a message that tells people what is happening and what to do

look.title: Why the Baker Bakes
look.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776
look.prompt: Benevolence means kindness. Smith says the baker bakes for his own reasons, not just to be nice. How does that still end up feeding you?

check.q: In June, Illinois strawberries cost less than in January. What is the price telling you?
choices: There are plenty of strawberries right now
check.why: A low price signals that a good is plentiful. In June, local farms are picking.

check.q: When corn prices are high, what do farmers tend to do?
check.why: A high price tells sellers to make more. Farmers plant more corn when it pays well.

check.q: What is one thing a price does NOT tell you?
choices: That a good is scarce right now
Whether a family can afford it
check.why: A price is a signal about how scarce a good is, but it says nothing about who can afford it.

lessons.title: Earn, Save, Spend, Give
lessons.mainIdea: Money you earn can be spent, saved for later or given away, and a budget helps you plan all three.
reading: Amara walks her neighbor's dog every afternoon. Each week she gets ten dollars. That is *earning*. People earn money by producing something, from a dog-walk to a day at a factory. Some people earn a wage by the hour. Some earn a salary by the year. Some own a business and keep what is left after costs.

Amara has a plan for her ten dollars. Four go in a jar for a bike she wants by summer. That is *saving*, keeping money now to use later. Five she spends on snacks and a book. One she puts in a can at her mosque for families who need food. That is giving. Many families give to a church, a temple or a food pantry.

Her plan is a *budget*. A budget is a written plan for money coming in and going out. It is simple math, but it changes lives. If Amara skipped the plan, she might spend all ten and never get the bike. Writing down the plan makes the opportunity cost of every snack easy to see.

words.d: to get money in return for work you do
to keep money now so you can use it later
a written plan for the money you will earn, spend, save and give

look.title: Amara's Weekly Plan
look.prompt: If the bike costs one hundred dollars, about how many weeks will Amara need? What could she change to get there sooner?

check.q: What is saving?
choices: Keeping money now to use later
check.why: Saving means holding on to money now so you can use it for something later.

check.q: Which of these is earning?
choices: Putting four dollars in a jar
Getting ten dollars for walking a dog
Dropping a dollar in a donation can
check.why: Earning is getting money in return for work. Amara works by walking the dog.

check.q: Why does a budget help Amara?
choices: It makes money grow by itself
It shows her plan so she reaches her goal
check.why: A budget is a plan. It makes the cost of each choice clear so she can reach the bike.

lessons.title: What a Bank Does
lessons.mainIdea: A bank keeps money safe, pays savers interest and lends money to people who need it now.
reading: A jar under the bed is a risky place for one hundred dollars. It can be lost, stolen or spent on a whim. So people take money to a *bank*. A bank is a business that keeps money safe. When you put money in, the bank writes down what it owes you. That is your account. You can take it out when you need it.

The bank does not leave your money in a pile. It lends most of it to other people. A family borrows to buy a house. A baker borrows to buy a bigger oven. They pay the money back over time, plus extra. That extra is *interest*. Interest is the price of using someone else's money.

The bank shares some of that interest with you for letting it use your savings. So a savings account grows a little every year. In the United States, a government program insures bank accounts up to a set amount. If a bank fails, savers still get their money. That rule came after many banks closed in the 1930s.

words.d: a business that keeps money safe, pays interest to savers and lends money
the extra money paid for using someone else's money

look.title: The Bakery Oven
look.text: Ms. Lopez owns a small bakery in Aurora. Her one oven is too small for all her orders. A new oven costs eight thousand dollars. She has two thousand saved. A bank offers to lend her the rest if she pays it back over three years with interest.
look.prompt: What does Ms. Lopez gain by borrowing? What does she risk? Where does the bank get the money to lend her?

check.q: Where does a bank get most of the money it lends?
check.why: A bank lends out money that savers have put in their accounts.

check.q: What is interest?
choices: Extra money paid for using someone else's money
check.why: Interest is the price of borrowing. Borrowers pay it, and savers earn some of it.

check.q: Why does a savings account grow a little each year?
choices: The bank pays interest on your savings
The bank adds coins for fun
Money always grows in a jar
check.why: The bank shares some interest with savers for letting it use their money.

lessons.title: Taxes and Public Goods
lessons.mainIdea: Taxes are money people pay to the government so it can provide public goods that everyone shares.
reading: Who paid for the street outside your school? Who pays the firefighters? No single family could buy a fire truck. So people pool their money through *taxes*. A tax is money that people and businesses must pay to a government. In Illinois, the state adds a sales tax to most things you buy. Workers pay a tax on what they earn. Homeowners pay a tax on their houses.

That money buys *public goods*. A public good is something everyone can use and no one can be kept from using, like a road, a park, a streetlight or clean air. A store cannot sell a streetlight one glow at a time. So governments provide it and taxes pay for it. Public schools, libraries and fire protection are paid the same way.

People argue about taxes all the time. Some say taxes are too high and take money families could use. Others say they are too low to fix roads and pay teachers. Both sides are talking about opportunity cost. Every tax dollar spent on one thing is not spent on another, and every dollar not collected is a public good not built.

words.d: money that people and businesses must pay to a government
something everyone can use and share, like a road or a park, that taxes pay for

look.title: The Power to Tax
look.text: The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States.
look.cite: United States Constitution, Article I, Section 8, 1787
look.prompt: What two reasons does the Constitution give for collecting taxes? Name one public good that fits each reason.

check.q: What is a tax?
choices: Money people must pay to a government
check.why: A tax is money that people and businesses are required to pay to a government.

check.q: Which of these is a public good?
check.why: A streetlight can be used by everyone and no one can be kept from using it.

check.q: Why do governments, not stores, provide streetlights?
choices: You cannot sell a streetlight's glow to one buyer
check.why: A public good cannot be sold one piece at a time, so taxes pay for it and everyone shares.

lessons.title: Corn Here, Oranges There
lessons.mainIdea: Specialization means doing what you do best, and regions specialize because of their land and climate.
reading: Drive across central Illinois in August and you see corn for miles. Fly to Florida and you see orange groves. Why not the other way around? Illinois has deep, dark soil and warm, rainy summers. Corn loves that. Florida is warm all winter. Orange trees die in a hard freeze, so they need a place that stays warm.

This is *specialization*. To specialize is to focus on the thing you can do best. Illinois specializes in corn and soybeans. Florida specializes in oranges. Idaho grows potatoes. Wisconsin makes cheese. Each place makes more by doing what its land and weather favor, instead of trying to grow a little of everything.

People specialize too. In Room 210, Maya is best with money and Devon is best with counting. So Maya keeps the box and Devon keeps the stock. A dentist does not bake her own bread. She fixes teeth all day and buys bread with what she earns. Specializing lets each person get very good at one thing.

words.d: focusing on making the thing you can do best
the usual weather of a place over many years

look.title: Average January Temperature
look.cite: National Weather Service climate normals, rounded
look.prompt: Orange trees die when it stays below freezing (32 degrees) for long. Use the numbers to explain why Florida, not Illinois, grows oranges.

check.q: Why does Illinois grow so much corn?
choices: It has deep soil and rainy summers
check.why: Corn grows well in the deep soil and warm, rainy summers of Illinois.

check.q: What is specialization?
choices: Focusing on what you do best
check.why: To specialize is to focus on the thing a person or place can do best.

check.q: Why do orange trees not grow well in Illinois?
choices: There is too much rain in summer
check.why: Orange trees die in a hard freeze. Illinois winters are far below freezing.

lessons.title: Why Trade Makes Both Sides Better
lessons.mainIdea: When people and places specialize and then trade, each ends up with more than it could make alone.
reading: Specialization only works if you can *trade*. To trade is to give something you have for something you want. Illinois sends corn and soybeans down the Mississippi River and across the world. Trucks and trains bring back oranges, cars, phones and shoes. Without trade, Illinois families would have no oranges at all.

Trade works because both sides win. Think of lunch. Sam has two bags of grapes and no crackers. Leo has two packs of crackers and no grapes. Each trades one for one. Now each has grapes and crackers. Nobody lost. The same thing happens when a country trades wheat for coffee.

Trade also has costs, and people argue about them. When a factory moves to another country, workers here can lose jobs. Goods get cheaper for consumers, but some producers are hurt. Both sides of that argument use real evidence. Knowing that trade makes the whole pie bigger does not tell you who gets each slice.

words.d: giving something you have in exchange for something you want
a good sent out of a place to be sold somewhere else

look.title: Two Farms, One Fence
look.text: Farm A can grow one thousand bushels of corn or two hundred bushels of apples in a year. Farm B, on a hilly slope, can grow two hundred bushels of corn or one thousand bushels of apples. Each farm wants both corn and apples.
look.prompt: What should each farm grow? What should they do next? Would they have more or less if each tried to grow both?

check.q: What is trade?
choices: Giving something you have for something you want
check.why: Trade is exchanging something you have for something you want.

check.q: Sam trades grapes for Leo's crackers. Who is better off?
check.why: Each gave up something they had extra of and got something they wanted. Both gained.

check.q: What is one real cost of trade the lesson mentions?
choices: Some workers here can lose jobs
check.why: When production moves elsewhere, some local workers lose jobs even though consumers pay less.

lessons.title: Starting Something New
lessons.mainIdea: An entrepreneur takes a risk to start a business that solves a problem people will pay for.
reading: In the early 1900s, a young man named Richard Sears sold watches by mail from a small railroad station. With a partner he built a company in Chicago that mailed a catalog to farm families. They could order a stove, a dress or even a whole house kit. Sears saw a problem, farm families far from stores, and found a way to solve it.

Sears was an *entrepreneur*. An entrepreneur is a person who starts a business, taking the *risk* that it might fail. Risk means the chance of losing something. Entrepreneurs put in their own money, time and sleep. Many businesses do fail. The ones that succeed create jobs and new goods and services.

You do not need to be famous to be one. The kids with the lemonade stand are entrepreneurs. So is the teenager who fixes phones after school. An entrepreneur looks for a need that is not being met, thinks of a way to meet it and tries. Room 210's store began that way, with one question: what do kids keep running out of?

words.d: a person who starts a business and takes the risk that it might fail
the chance of losing something, like money or time

look.title: The Problem on Your Block
look.text: On Tasha's block, older neighbors cannot carry heavy grocery bags up their stairs. Tasha and two friends have a wagon and free time on Saturdays. They think they could charge two dollars per trip. But they will need a sign, and they might spend a Saturday waiting with no customers.
look.prompt: What need did Tasha spot? What is her risk? What would you tell her to find out before she starts?

check.q: What is an entrepreneur?
choices: A person who only buys goods
A person who starts a business and takes a risk
check.why: An entrepreneur starts a business, knowing it might fail.

check.q: What problem did Richard Sears solve?
choices: Farm families lived far from stores
check.why: Sears mailed a catalog so farm families far from stores could order what they needed.

check.q: What does risk mean in this lesson?
check.why: Risk is the chance that you lose money, time or effort if the business fails.

review.q: A farmer grows wheat and a mill grinds it into flour. Both are what?
review.why: Producers make goods or do work that others want. Both the farmer and the mill are producers.

review.q: Which of these is a good, not a service?
review.why: A good is a thing you can touch and take home. A bike is a good.

review.q: Why can't Maya buy both the notebook and the stickers?
review.why: Scarcity means she does not have enough money for everything she wants.

review.q: On test day the school store ran out of pencils. What was happening?
review.why: A shortage is when buyers want more than sellers have at that price.

review.q: The price of strawberries falls in June. What does the price signal?
review.why: A low price signals that a good is easy to get right now.

review.q: Money paid for using someone else's money is called what?
review.why: Interest is the price of borrowing. Banks pay it to savers and charge it to borrowers.

review.q: Which is the best example of a public good paid for by taxes?
review.why: A park can be used by everyone and is paid for by taxes, so it is a public good.

review.q: Why do Illinois and Florida grow different crops?
choices: Their land and climate favor different crops
The government tells them what to grow
review.why: Places specialize in what their soil and climate favor: corn in Illinois, oranges in Florida.
